items.item: Why a tiny, highly selective outer side with an indexed inner side makes nested loop win by a wide margin, measured directly rather than asserted
Why hash join wins an unfiltered equi-join when neither a small outer side nor a free sort order is available
That merge join measured as the most expensive of the three on this topic's own schema is an honest, reported finding, not a general ranking of the three algorithms
Reading a hash join's batch count directly off EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) as the signal that it spilled to disk, rather than inferring it from timing alone
What enable_nestloop=off actually does under the hood (repricing alternatives, not forbidding nested loop), confirmed by reading the planner's own inflated cost for the disallowed paths
Grace/hybrid hash join partitioning as the general mechanism behind a batch count, named but deliberately left to its own later topic rather than claimed here without a quoted source
Block nested loop (batching outer rows to amortize an unindexed inner re-scan) as a real technique this topic's own measured examples didn't need, since an index was always available
Why a query joined with a non-equality predicate was never a hash-join or merge-join candidate in the first place, as a production diagnostic rule
work_mem's per-operation, per-session nature, and why raising it globally to fix one query can multiply total memory use across concurrent sessions
Why enable_nestloop=off is a diagnostic tool rather than a production fix, since it discourages nested loop even on the small, highly selective joins where it's genuinely the fastest choice
